sentences.text: Yingshanosaurus was a medium-sized, slow-moving quadrupedal herbivore that lived in what is now Southwestern China. This dinosaur measured between four and five meters in length.
Its backbone included nine dorsal vertebrae and a sacrum made of five firmly fused vertebrae. Four of these sacral vertebrae were solidly fused with the ilium of the pelvis.

The holotype, which is the specimen the species is based on, contains five nearly complete osteoderms from various body regions. The largest of these is an 80 cm long parascapular spine located on the shoulder.

Anatomical features include transverse processes projecting at an angle of about 60 degrees relative to the neural spine. It possessed seven haemal arches with typical stegosaur anatomy, differing from the inverted T-shape of Kentrosaurus. The neural spines of its dorsal vertebrae were plate-shaped with a transversely expanded top.
Early reconstructions incorrectly placed Yingshanosaurus's large shoulder spines near the pelvic girdle as 'parasacral spines' before Gigantspinosaurus clarified their position.
The genus name Yingshanosaurus is derived from the locality of Yingshan, while the species name refers to the location of the locality, Jichuan.

A partial skeleton was discovered in 1983 when a villager in Jichuan, Sichuan Province, China, found it while digging a house foundation. A stegosaur skeleton was excavated in Sichuan in 1983 by a team led by Wan Jihou. The discovery was reported by Zhou Shiwu in 1984.

The only known species, Yingshanosaurus jichuanensis, was named and described in 1994. Zhu Songlin formally described the genus and species in 1994, designating the skeleton as holotype specimen CV00722.
Like all stegosaurs, Yingshanosaurus was a herbivorous dinosaur.
The exact purpose of Yingshanosaurus's osteoderms is a subject of debate among scientists. Researchers suggest the plates may have been used for display, species recognition, or thermoregulation.

Zhu noted that the femur-to-tibia ratio of Yingshanosaurus is more similar to Kentrosaurus than to Stegosaurus or Dacentrurus. Zhu classified Yingshanosaurus within the family Stegosauridae and the subfamily Stegosaurinae. The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Yingshanosaurus as Stegosauridae.

Some researchers argue the name should be considered invalid because the original description was difficult to find. It was assumed for a long time that the name Yingshanosaurus would remain a nomen nudum due to insufficient description, despite the conference being published in 1986. Although the validity of the name has been reaffirmed, it is rarely cited in international scientific literature.
